result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.add_prism_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a prism graph to the current graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L5029-L5137){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_prism_graph( n, type=None, label=True, rel=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Prism graph](/assets/graphs/add-prism-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three prism graphs side by side for n=3, 4, and 5, each drawn as an outer n-cycle around an inner n-cycle with n rungs joining matching nodes. That gives 2n nodes and 3n edges: 6 and 9, 8 and 12, 10 and 15." width="100%"} Creates two parallel n-cycles connected by n vertical edges, forming a 3D prism structure when visualized. The result has `2n` nodes and `3n` edges (`n` per cycle plus `n` "rungs"), and every node has degree `3`. With `n=3` this is the triangular prism and with `n=4` it is the cube graph. The "top" cycle is created first, then the "bottom" cycle, and the rungs join the `i`-th top node to the `i`-th bottom node. In a directed graph each cycle runs in one direction (from each node to the next) and every rung points from top to bottom. The prism is appended to the graph without touching or connecting to existing nodes. Prism graphs are a compact example of a 3-regular (cubic) graph, which makes them useful for: - testing algorithms on regular, symmetric graphs where all nodes look alike - modeling ring-shaped networks with a redundant parallel ring (e.g. dual-ring topologies) - illustrative examples of planar, Hamiltonian, polyhedral graphs ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes in each cycle. Must be at least `3`; the graph will have `2n` nodes. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), nodes are labelled with a number plus a suffix marking their cycle: `"1_top"` to `"n_top"`, then `"(n+1)_bottom"` to `"(2n)_bottom"` (e.g. `"5_bottom"` for `n=4`). The number is the node's ID, and a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, nodes are created without labels. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge (cycle edges and rungs alike). If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is less than `3`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A prism graph joins two parallel `n`-cycles with `n` "rung" edges connecting corresponding nodes, so it always has `2n` nodes and `3n` edges (`n` edges per cycle, plus `n` rungs). Here `n=5` gives `10` nodes and `15` edges: ::: {#99f3c98e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_prism_graph(5) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (10, 15) ``` ::: ::: The labels show the structure directly. With `n=4` (the cube graph), the first four edges form the top cycle, the next four the bottom cycle, and the last four are the rungs joining `"1_top"` to `"5_bottom"`, and so on: ::: {#81abd3ea .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} cube = ec.Graph().add_prism_graph(n=4) cube.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['1_top--2_top', '2_top--3_top', '3_top--4_top', '4_top--1_top', '5_bottom--6_bottom', '6_bottom--7_bottom', '7_bottom--8_bottom', '8_bottom--5_bottom', '1_top--5_bottom', '2_top--6_bottom', '3_top--7_bottom', '4_top--8_bottom'] ``` ::: ::: Every node in a prism graph has exactly three neighbors -- two in its own cycle and one across the rung: ::: {#aa8cfbf1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} {cube.get_degree(nid) for nid in cube.get_node_ids()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {3} ``` ::: :::
